units.title: Deborah
units.subtitle: A prophet, a general, a tent pin, and a song

lessons.title: Deborah (1): Under the palm tree
lessons.check_note: Megillah 14a-b, Esther Rabbah 5:4 and Zohar Vayikra 47:328 (Soncino) read on Sefaria 11/12. English: JPS Tanakh Gender-Sensitive.

cards.title: A prophet who leads
cards.body: Israel is oppressed by a Canaanite king. Its leader at that time is a woman: **Deborah**, prophet and judge.

cards.q: According to the Talmud, why is Deborah called "wife of Lappidoth"?
choices: She made wicks for the Sanctuary

cards.gloss: "Deborah, wife of Lappidoth, was a prophet" (4:4).

cards.title: A woman of flames
cards.body: The Talmud counts **seven prophetesses**: Sarah, Miriam, **Deborah**, Hannah, Abigail, Huldah and Esther. Why "wife of Lappidoth"? Because she made **wicks for the Sanctuary**, and from the flames, לַפִּידוֹת, she was called a woman of flames.

cards.q: Why does the Talmud call Deborah "a woman of flames"?
cards.why: Before she lit up Israel as a judge, she made **light for the Sanctuary**.

cards.gloss: "She used to sit under the Palm of Deborah" (4:5).

cards.title: Why under a palm tree?
cards.body: **Rabbi Shimon ben Avshalom**: she judged **out in the open**, visible to all, so she would never be alone behind closed doors with the men who came to her. Or: a palm tree has **one heart**, a single trunk, and so did Israel in her generation, one heart turned to their Father in Heaven.

cards.q: In Megillah 14a, what is one reason Deborah judged under a palm tree?
choices: To judge in the open, visible to everyone
Because it was sacred to Baal
wrong_why: The Talmud gives a deeper reason.

cards.title: How the rabbis saw her
cards.body: The Bible simply names Deborah prophet and judge. Later readers argued. **Esther Rabbah**: when Israel was crushed, who was fitting for the moment? **Deborah**. **Rav Nachman** calls her haughty, because she sent for Barak instead of going to him. The **Zohar** goes further: "Woe to the generation which could only find a female to be its judge!"

cards.q: Which source says Deborah was the one "fitting" for her moment?
cards.why: Rabbinic voices **disagree** about her; Esther Rabbah praises her.
wrong_why: The Zohar laments a woman judge.

cards.prompt: The Bible calls Deborah a prophet and leader; later readers argued about her. When have you seen someone's leadership doubted for who they were rather than what they did?

points: Megillah 14a: **a woman of flames**, wicks for the Sanctuary.
Judging **under the palm**, in the open; one heart.
Rabbinic views **differ**: fitting, haughty, or a sign of a weak generation.

lessons.title: Deborah (2): Barak and Jael
lessons.check_note: Nazir 23b read on Sefaria 11/12 (its sexual reading of 5:27 left out).

cards.title: Not without you
cards.body: Deborah tells **Barak** to lead ten thousand men against **Sisera**, the Canaanite general. Barak has one condition.

cards.q: Barak would not go to battle unless Deborah came with him.
cards.why: "If you will go with me, I will go; if not, I will not go" (4:8).

cards.gloss: "GOD will deliver Sisera into the hands of a woman" (4:9). Which woman? Not Deborah, as it turns out.

cards.q: Into whose hands does Deborah say Sisera will fall?
cards.why: **A woman's** hand, and the story will name her.

cards.title: Jael
cards.body: Sisera's army is routed and he flees on foot to the tent of **Jael**, wife of Heber the Kenite. She invites him in, gives him milk, and covers him. When he sleeps, she takes a tent pin and a mallet.

cards.title: For the sake of Heaven
cards.body: **Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak**: a transgression done **for the sake of Heaven** is equal to a mitzvah done not for its own sake. His proof is Jael: "Most blessed of women in tents." Who are the women in the tent? **Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel and Leah**. Jael, who did what she had to do to stop Sisera, is ranked with the matriarchs.

cards.q: In Nazir 23b, who are the "women in tents" Jael is blessed above?

cards.prompt: Barak would not go alone, and the victory went to two women. Who do you need beside you to do something hard?

points: Barak: "**If you will go with me, I will go**" (4:8).
Sisera falls **into the hands of a woman** (4:9).

lessons.title: Deborah (3): Awake, sing
lessons.check_note: Pesachim 66b read on Sefaria 11/12. L'cha Dodi line from data/prayers.json.

cards.title: A victory song
cards.body: After the battle, **Deborah and Barak sing**.

cards.q: According to Pesachim 66b, why did Deborah's prophecy leave her for a time?

cards.he: אָנֹכִי לַֽיהֹוָה אָנֹכִי אָשִׁירָה אֲזַמֵּר לַֽיהֹוָה
cards.gloss: "I will sing, will sing to GOD" (5:3).

cards.he: עַד שַׁקַּמְתִּי דְּבוֹרָה שַׁקַּמְתִּי אֵם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
cards.gloss: "Arose, O mother, in Israel!" (5:7). The JPS reads the verb as said **to** Deborah. The Talmud reads it as Deborah speaking of herself: **until I arose**.

cards.title: A mother in Israel
cards.body: **Rav Yehuda** in the name of **Rav**: whoever acts haughtily, if a sage, loses wisdom; if a prophet, **loses prophecy**. From Deborah: "until I, Deborah, arose, I arose a mother in Israel." For praising herself, her prophecy left her, so later she had to be told, "Awake, awake, Deborah."

cards.q: How does Pesachim 66b explain "Awake, awake, Deborah"?
choices: Her prophecy had left her after she praised herself
She had fallen asleep after the battle
cards.why: Pride **dimmed** her prophecy; the song **wakes** it.

cards.he: עוּרִי עוּרִי דְּבוֹרָה עוּרִי עוּרִי דַּבְּרִי־שִׁיר
cards.gloss: "Awake, awake, O Deborah! Awake, awake, strike up the chant!" (5:12).

cards.body: Every Friday night, **L'cha Dodi** borrows Deborah's words: עוּרִי עוּרִי שִׁיר דַּבֵּרִי.

cards.prompt: Deborah calls herself "a mother in Israel," and the Talmud warns against self-praise. How do you tell healthy pride from too much?

points: "Arose, O mother, in Israel": **you** arose, or **I** arose?
"**Awake, awake**": in L'cha Dodi every Shabbat.

lessons.title: Deborah (4): Sisera's mother
lessons.check_note: Rosh Hashanah 33b and Megillah 10b read on Sefaria (33b on 11/12).

cards.title: At the window
cards.body: Deborah's song does not end with the victors. It ends in the enemy's house, with **Sisera's mother**, waiting at the window.

cards.q: The Talmud learns the sound of the shofar's teruah from the crying of Sisera's mother.
cards.why: Rosh Hashanah 33b defines the sound by her **wailing**.

cards.he: בְּעַד הַחַלּוֹן נִשְׁקְפָה וַתְּיַבֵּב אֵם סִֽיסְרָא
cards.gloss: "Through the window peered Sisera’s mother" (5:28). Her crying is וַתְּיַבֵּב.

cards.title: The sound of the shofar
cards.body: The Torah calls Rosh Hashanah **a day of teruah**, and the Aramaic translation calls it a day of **yevava**. What is yevava? The Talmud answers from this verse: Sisera's mother **wailed**, וַתְּיַבֵּב. One view hears **moaning sighs** (shevarim), another **whimpers** (teruot). The shofar's sounds are measured by **an enemy mother's cry**.

cards.q: In Rosh Hashanah 33b, how does the Talmud define the shofar's sound?
choices: By the crying of Sisera's mother
By the trumpets of Barak's army
cards.why: The shofar sounds like **a mother's crying**.

cards.title: Not rejoicing
cards.body: Compare the Sea: when the Egyptians drowned, God stopped the angels from singing, because they too were **the work of My hands**.

cards.gloss: "And the land was tranquil forty years" (5:31).

cards.q: How does the story of Deborah end?
choices: The land was tranquil forty years

cards.prompt: The song ends with a mother waiting for a son who will not come home, and the shofar still carries her cry. Can you hold victory and grief at the same time?

points: The song ends with **Sisera's mother** at the window (5:28).
Rosh Hashanah 33b: the shofar's sound is **her cry**.
Megillah 10b: God does not rejoice when enemies drown.
